```{=html}
<div class="paper-grid">
<article class="paper">
  <h3 class="paper-title">The Ebb after the Wave: Explaining the Diverging Electoral Fortunes of European Green Parties after 2019</h3>
  <p class="paper-meta">Puqiu Zhao · Work in progress · 2026</p>
  <p class="paper-tags">Green Parties · Electoral Politics · Crisis</p>
  <blockquote class="paper-quote">Why did the crises lead to a decline in support for some Green parties, while others maintained or even increased their support?</blockquote>
  <div class="paper-actions">
    <a class="paper-btn" href="ebb-after-the-wave.html">Project page</a>
    <a class="paper-btn" href="ebb-after-the-wave.html#literature">Literature</a>
    <details class="paper-abstract">
      <summary>Read abstract</summary>
      <p>European Green parties’ electoral performance provides an important barometer of public attitudes towards climate change and societal demand for further climate action. European Parliament elections are particularly valuable because, as second-order elections, they allow voters to express their preferences more sincerely. The 2019 election marked a significant breakthrough for Green parties, widely associated with the European Green Deal. However, most Green parties experienced declining vote shares in 2024.</p>
      <p>Existing studies explain the universal decline from the environmental and economic trade-off from the demand and spatial and issue competition from the supply. However, we still do not know why some Green parties have declined while others have gained ground. The paper offers a parsimonious theoretical explanation based on the sanctioning and selection logic, and explains the variation through three main mechanisms: strategic policy changes by Green parties, heterogeneous external shocks, and signals sent by competing political parties. We empirically examine these mechanisms and primarily find that heterogeneous external shocks alone cannot account for the divergence. The paper identifies the party characteristics that enable Green parties to sustain electoral support during the economic crisis.</p>
    </details>
  </div>
</article>
<article class="paper">
  <h3 class="paper-title">Explaining Continuity and Change in Chinese Strategic Culture, 1992&ndash;2026: A Realist-Constructivist Analysis</h3>
  <p class="paper-meta">Yingjian Li, Puqiu Zhao · Work in progress · 2026</p>
  <p class="paper-tags">Strategic Culture · China · Text Analysis</p>
  <blockquote class="paper-quote">How far has Chinese strategic culture changed since the end of the Cold War, and what explains its continuity and change?</blockquote>
  <div class="paper-actions">
    <details class="paper-abstract">
      <summary>Read abstract</summary>
      <p>Drawing on the realist-constructivist Four Pathways Model (Li and Meyer, 2026), this paper examines Chinese strategic culture between 1992 and 2026. It tests three pathways of change: national security crises, international environmental change and elite change. The analysis considers how pressures arising through these pathways interact with cultural change agents and structural inertia to produce change or sustain established strategic orientations.</p>
      <p>The study uses quantitative text coding in R to trace changes across five dimensions: threat perceptions, goals for the use of force, preferred modes of cooperation, civil-military relations and legal-ethical constraints. Its sources are authoritative Chinese-language texts publicly articulating security and defence policy, including Party Congress reports, government work reports and defence white papers. The analysis examines the timing and extent of change across the dimensions and the role of different pathways in explaining these changes. By applying a framework informed by European strategic culture research to China, the paper assesses its explanatory value in a different political and historical context. It aims to refine the framework and provide an updated, longitudinal account of the evolution of Chinese strategic culture.</p>
    </details>
  </div>
</article>
</div>
```
